The Black-faced Antthrush (Formicarius analis) is a secretive ground-dwelling bird of Neotropical lowland forests, and its life history is characterized by a slow pace typical of many understory insectivores. Neonates emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] after approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days], a developmental period consistent with other members of the Formicariidae. At hatching, these altricial nestlings possess a remarkably low initial body mass of only 6.8 grams [Ww0 = 6.8 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves available to support early growth. This minimal birth weight imposes a significant energetic demand on the parents, who must provision the chick intensively during the initial weeks of life. The rapid growth trajectory that follows is crucial for the nestling to reach the developmental milestones necessary for fledging within the species' relatively short nesting cycle, thereby minimizing the risk of predation that is a constant pressure for ground-nesting passerines.

Under the thermal conditions that typify the active metabolic and foraging periods of this species, around 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the nestling period culminates in fledging at 18 days since birth [tx = 18 days since birth]. This relatively early departure from the nest represents a trade-off between the benefits of prolonged parental care and the escalating risk of nest predation in the leaf-litter habitat. Following fledging, the juvenile bird enters a phase of rapid growth and behavioral development. The species attains sexual maturity relatively quickly for a bird of its size, with puberty occurring at 40.5 days since birth [tp = 40.5 days since birth] when maintained at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. However, the onset of gonadal activation does not immediately translate into reproductive activity, as individuals require additional time to establish territories and secure mates in the dense understory.

The first successful breeding event, or first brood, is typically deferred well beyond the point of physiological puberty. Under the same thermal conditions typical of this species (41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]), the time since birth at first brood is approximately 1.1 years [tR = approximately 1.1 years]. This considerable delay between puberty and first reproduction likely reflects the challenges of territory acquisition in a saturated habitat, as well as the need to attain full adult body mass before committing to the energetic costs of egg production and incubation. Fully grown adults reach an asymptotic mass averaging 62.55 grams [Wwi = 62.55 grams], whereas males plateau at a slightly lower 60.85 grams [Wwi = 60.85 grams], a subtle sexual size dimorphism that may relate to differential energetic investment in reproductive roles.

Reproductive output in the Black-faced Antthrush is modest, consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high fecundity. Females typically lay two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], and annual breeding frequency is limited to approximately one clutch each year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch each year]. This low annual reproductive rate, averaging about two offspring per year, is typical of Neotropical forest insectivores constrained by food availability and high nest predation rates. The species' maximum recorded longevity, when measured at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], reaches 10 years [am = 10 years], which is a substantial lifespan for a bird of this body size. This extended adult survival, coupled with low annual fecundity, reinforces a slow life-history continuum that buffers population stability against stochastic environmental fluctuations in the understory.

Basal metabolic rate in the Black-faced Antthrush has been measured through respirometry trials conducted at a core body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. The maximum basal metabolic rate recorded for this species is 112.73 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 112.73 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the energetic cost of thermoregulation and basic physiological maintenance in a thermally stable but humid forest floor environment at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This metabolic expenditure is moderate compared to sympatric antbirds of similar mass, aligning with the species' relatively sedentary foraging strategy, which involves slow, deliberate movements through the leaf litter in search of arthropods. The interplay between a decadelong lifespan, deferred first reproduction, and low fecundity situates Formicarius analis among the more K-selected members of its guild, where physiological efficiency and adult persistence take precedence over rapid population turnover in the competitive understory environment.
